n: After dealing with the Philistines, Saul hears that David is in the wilderness of En-gedi and resumes the hunt.
Saul takes three thousand elite soldiers to search the rugged cliffs where wild goats live. David has only about six hundred men.

f.w: the rocks of the wild goats
f.g: The steep cliffs around En-gedi, home to ibex.

n: Saul comes to a cave near some sheep pens and goes in to relieve himself — unaware that David and his men are hiding deep inside that very cave.

f.g: A polite Hebrew expression for relieving oneself.
sheep pens, often built near cave mouths

n: David's men urge him to seize this God-given chance to kill his enemy. David creeps up and secretly cuts off a corner of Saul's robe instead.

f.g: The hem or corner of the robe could symbolize royal authority.

n: Even this small act troubles David's conscience. Cutting the king's robe felt like an attack on the Lord's anointed. A sensitive conscience is a gift.
David refuses to harm Saul because he is the Lord's anointed. He leaves Saul's fate to God rather than taking the throne by force.
David restrains his men and won't let them attack Saul. Saul leaves the cave and goes on his way, unaware of how close he came to death.
David follows Saul out and calls, “My lord the king!” When Saul turns, David bows to the ground in respect — honoring Saul's office even while Saul tries to kill him.
David asks why Saul listens to people who say David wants to harm him. He tactfully blames advisers rather than Saul himself.
David points out that the Lord put Saul in his hands in the cave. Some urged him to kill Saul, but he refused because Saul is the Lord's anointed.
Calling Saul “my father,” David holds up the piece of robe as proof: he could have killed Saul but didn't. He is innocent, yet Saul hunts him.

f.g: A respectful address; Saul was also his father-in-law.

n: David leaves justice to the Lord: let God judge between them and vindicate him, but David himself will never harm Saul.

f.w: The LORD judge between me and thee

n: David quotes an old proverb: wicked deeds come from wicked people. Since he is not wicked, he will not do evil to Saul.
With humble self-description, David asks why the king of Israel is chasing someone as insignificant as a dead dog or a flea.

f.w: a dead dog, after a flea
f.g: Images of something worthless and harmless.

n: David again commits his cause to the Lord as judge and defender, asking God to rescue him from Saul's hand.
Deeply moved, Saul cries out, “Is this your voice, my son David?” and weeps aloud. For a moment the old Saul resurfaces.
Saul admits David is more righteous than he, because David repaid evil with good.
Saul acknowledges that David has treated him well by sparing his life when he could have killed him.
Who lets an enemy go unharmed when he finds him? Saul prays that the Lord will reward David for his goodness.
Saul openly admits that David will surely be king and that Israel's kingdom will be established through him.
Saul asks David to swear not to wipe out his descendants or erase his family name — a common practice of new dynasties.

f.w: thou wilt not cut off my seed

n: David swears the oath. Saul goes home, but David, knowing Saul's moods can change, returns to his stronghold.
